stories.brief: A Grapevine column uses Reuven Rivlin as the central public figure, with attention to his background and civic voice.

sources.title: Past Presidents of Israel - Reuven Rivlin
Rivlin, Reuven
Knesset elects Reuven Rivlin as State of Israel`s 10th president
Grapevine: Kafka in Jerusalem
GRAPEVINE: The president is grounded
Grapevine January 15, 2021: Rivlin hosts a meeting of the ‘tribes’

storyBeats: Reuven Rivlin was born in Jerusalem on September 9, 1939, into a deeply rooted Jerusalem family with multiple generations in the Land of Israel.
He studied law at the Hebrew University and qualified as a lawyer before moving into national politics.
His public career included work as an intelligence officer, Jerusalem municipal councillor, chairman of the Jerusalem branch of the Herut movement, and several senior party and civic roles.
He served as Speaker of the Knesset in two separate terms, first from 2003 to 2006 and again from 2009 to 2013.
In June 2014, the Knesset elected Rivlin as Israel’s 10th president.
The president’s office later described him as coming from a Jerusalemite family and as the tenth president, linking his public identity to both heritage and national office.
During his presidency, Rivlin repeatedly spoke about the divisions among Israel’s social groups and sought to frame public life around dialogue between what he called the country’s ‘tribes’.
That approach made him a visible civic figure beyond the formal limits of the presidency, especially in the context of repeated elections and national polarization.
By September 2026, he remained a public reference point in Israeli political and civic commentary, with press coverage marking his 87th birthday and treating him as an enduring public voice.

stories.brief: The history of Maskit follows Israel’s first fashion house and its revival as a brand tied to design, craftsmanship, and national style. The subject is an Israeli fashion company with a long cultural-industrial life.

sources.title: About Us
Maskit 10/30/70
MASKIT: The comeback of Israel’s first fashion house
Israel’s first fashion house and first motion picture

storyBeats: Maskit was founded in 1954 by Ruth Dayan as a government-backed initiative to create work for new immigrants and preserve traditional crafts from diverse communities in Israel.
From the start, the house combined local craft techniques with fashion production rather than importing a fully foreign style model.
Maskit developed into Israel’s first and only haute couture fashion house, with designs linked to local culture and artisan work.
Its clothing drew attention from major international fashion figures and was sold through luxury retailers abroad.
By the second half of the twentieth century, the company had expanded into a network of boutiques across Israel.
In the 1960s, the company shifted toward mass, cost-effective production, reflecting a major change in its business direction.
That later commercial direction did not prevent decline; the historical exhibition on Maskit notes that the brand’s first long era ended in closure in 1994.
The brand was revived in 2014 by Sharon and Nir Tal as a privately owned haute couture label.
After the revival, Maskit pursued contemporary fashion while presenting itself as a continuation of Israeli craftsmanship and heritage.
The museum exhibition framing its history uses the dates 1954, 1994, and 2014 as the major milestones of the company’s arc.

stories.brief: Annie Dillard’s obituary centers on her career as a Pulitzer-winning writer and essayist whose work connected nature, spirituality, and close observation. The subject is her literary influence and the shape of her writing life.

sources.title: Annie Dillard, Pulitzer-winning author of 'Pilgrim at Tinker Creek,' dies at 81
Annie Dillard
Dillard, Annie 1945-

storyBeats: Annie Dillard was born Meta Ann Doak in Pittsburgh in 1945 and later studied at Hollins College, earning both a BA and an MA.
Her early literary formation was shaped by writers such as Henry David Thoreau and Walt Whitman, whose influence is noted in biographical sources on her work.
She published her first poetry collection, Tickets for a Prayer Wheel, before the book that made her reputation.
In 1974, Pilgrim at Tinker Creek won the Pulitzer Prize and established her as a major American prose writer.
The book grew out of close observation of the natural world and became associated with her sustained interest in theology, philosophy, and the physical world.
She went on to publish An American Childhood, For the Time Being, The Maytrees, and The Abundance, extending her range across memoir, essay, and fiction.
She also edited anthologies, including Best American Essays 1988 and Modern American Memoirs.
Her work earned additional honors including National Endowment for the Humanities recognition in 2014 and membership in major American arts academies.
On September 17, 2026, AP reported that Dillard had died at age 81, recasting her career as a completed body of work rather than an ongoing literary career.

stories.brief: The history of ATA as an Israeli clothing brand and factory traces mass garment production, immigrant labor, and a symbol of early Israeli everyday dress. The central subject is the business and its industrial role.

sources.title: Ata Textile Company LTD - Beit Fisher Archive
ATA
Efforts to Save Ata Textile Mills
That’s how it happened

storyBeats: ATA began as an industrial textile company in Kiryat Ata, with the plant operating from 1934 to 1985.
The factory produced clothing, textiles for the home, and goods sold through stores and businesses across Israel.
ATA grew into a recognizable industrial employer and a producer of everyday clothing and uniforms in the developing Israeli market.
The company’s archive records not only products and design sketches but also social life around the factory and the people who worked there.
By the 1980s, ATA entered bankruptcy after losing its largest overseas customer, marking the collapse of its earlier industrial model.
The company’s decline turned ATA from a living factory into a remembered part of Israeli industrial and labor history.
The Beit Fisher Museum in Kiryat Ata later preserved ATA materials, and the National Library of Israel digitized a representative sample of those records in 2019-2020.
The archive includes clothing items, marketing material, press clippings, and design documentation donated by the founders’ sons and former workers.
In 2016, ATA was re-established as a fashion brand, giving the historic name a new commercial life after the original factory era ended.

stories.brief: AI-generated dialog. Two neighbors, Yael and Amir, are talking outside their building because Amir found a warning notice on his car and thinks the permit may have expired. Yael asks whether he parked in the guest spot or the resident spot, and Amir says he is not sure because he rushed out before work. They walk to the lot, check the sticker and the notice, and realize the car is fine but the permit number was written incorrectly in the building register. Amir worries the towing company may already have been called, so Yael suggests calling the management office right away. The office confirms the mistake, asks them to send a photo, and cancels the pickup request. In the end, Amir keeps the car where it is, the notice is cleared, and they decide to update the parking list that evening.

stories.brief: An employee is preparing handouts before a team presentation when the printer starts producing crooked pages and one section comes out missing. They ask a coworker whether the file was sent in the right format, and the coworker says it looked fine on the screen but may have the wrong margins. After a quick check, they notice the PDF is still open in the wrong version, so they re-export it and try again. There is still not much time, so they decide to print fewer copies, staple them by hand, and hand out the slides only to the people who need them. In the end, the presentation starts on time, the handouts are usable, and they make a note to check the final file before printing next time.

AI-generated dialog. Two friends, Dana and Niv, are at a supermarket self-checkout after work. Dana scans a few items and notices that one price is much higher than the shelf label, so she asks Niv whether she read the label wrong or whether the store changed it again. Niv checks the app and the receipt screen, and they realize the cashier lane nearby is closed, so they need a staff member for help. A store employee comes over, looks at the shelf tag, and confirms the discount was still supposed to apply. Dana asks if they can switch the item for a similar one, but Niv says they should wait a minute because the system may fix it faster. The employee corrects the price, they finish paying, and in the end they leave with the cheaper item and enough time to catch the bus.

AI-generated dialog. Two roommates, Maya and Omer, are in the apartment kitchen after dinner. Maya asks whether Omer already washed the pan, and Omer says he did not have time because he came home late and only ate quickly. They notice the sink is getting full, and Maya says the dishes cannot wait until morning because someone needs the sink for breakfast. Omer agrees, but he asks whether they can split the job instead of one person doing everything. Maya says yes, as long as he dries the dishes and takes out the trash afterward. They work through it together, clear the counter, and decide to write a simple weekday chore plan on the fridge.

AI-generated dialog. A patient and a clinic receptionist are speaking because the patient called to ask about test results that still have not arrived. The receptionist checks the file and says the doctor reviewed the results but wants one more referral before making a final plan. The patient asks whether this means something is wrong, and the receptionist explains that the doctor simply wants a second test and a clearer note from the lab. The patient is frustrated because they already waited all week, so they ask if the referral can be sent by email today. The receptionist says yes, but only after the doctor signs it, so the patient agrees to wait for the message and then book the next step. In the end, the referral is sent, the patient understands the delay, and they can move forward with the next appointment.

A person arrives home late in a taxi and discovers that the building entrance is locked tighter than usual because the side door is under repair. They call a neighbor from the car and ask whether the main code still works or whether someone left the lobby key with security. The neighbor checks the message thread, realizes the code changed earlier in the evening, and walks downstairs to open the door. While waiting, the passenger asks the driver not to leave yet because they still need to carry up two bags and a laptop. Once the door is open, they get inside, thank the neighbor, and save the updated code so they do not get stuck outside again.

AI-generated dialog. Two partners, Tomer and Liat, are talking by phone because Tomer just found out he must stay at work longer than expected. Liat asks whether it is only a short delay or if the meeting may run into the evening, and Tomer says it is probably another hour, maybe more. They had planned dinner outside, so Liat says she can wait a little, but not until very late because she still has an early morning. Tomer suggests cancelling the reservation and getting something simple near home instead, but Liat checks the restaurant policy and warns there may be a fee if they cancel too late. They discuss a few options, decide to move the booking to a later time, and order a quick snack while Tomer finishes work. In the end, they keep the dinner plan, avoid the fee, and agree to message earlier next time when work runs late.

AI-generated dialog. Two coworkers, Dana and Ido, are meeting at a train station after work because Dana’s ticket QR code will not scan and the departure platform has just changed. Dana says she is already at the gate, while Ido asks whether the app shows an error or only a frozen screen. They check the ticket details, realize Dana opened the wrong booking, and notice the train is leaving from a different platform than usual. Ido suggests using the help machine, but Dana worries there is no time because the train is boarding now. A station employee confirms the ticket is valid, reprints a backup code, and tells them which platform to use.
